title: Undefined Behaviour & Common Pitfalls
html:
Undefined behaviour (UB) means the standard places no requirements on what happens. The program may crash, work by accident, or be “optimised” into something surprising. Know the usual suspects.

Undefined behaviour — the result of executing an operation the standard doesn't define — e.g. out-of-bounds access or signed overflow. Compilers assume UB never happens and optimise on that assumption, so its effects can show up far from the bug.

The usual suspects

UBExampleTool that catches it
Out-of-bounds accessv[v.size()], arr[10] on int arr[10]ASan, .at(), -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS
Use after free / danglingReference into a vector that grew, returning &localASan
Uninitialised readint x; if (x) …-Wall (sometimes), MSan, Valgrind
Signed integer overflowINT_MAX + 1UBSan
Null dereference*p with p == nullptrCrash / UBSan
Data raceTwo threads write a non-atomic variableTSan
Shift out of range1 << 32 on a 32-bit int, negative shiftUBSan
Strict-aliasing violation*(int*)&someFloat-fstrict-aliasing warnings; use memcpy/bit_cast
Modifying a const objectconst_cast then write—
Missing return in a non-void functionFalling off the end-Wreturn-type (error in clang)

Sanitizers find UB for you

Classic pitfalls (not all UB, all bugs)

Watch out

“It works on my machine” means nothing for UB. A different compiler, optimisation level or input can change the behaviour. Always test with -Wall -Wextra and sanitizers on.

What's the difference between undefined, unspecified and implementation-defined behaviour?

Undefined: no requirements at all (out-of-bounds, signed overflow). Unspecified: one of several valid outcomes, not documented (order of evaluating function arguments). Implementation-defined: one outcome the implementation must document (sizeof(long), whether char is signed).

Why doesn't C++ just check array bounds?

Zero-overhead philosophy: checks cost time in tight loops, and many accesses are provably in range. C++ gives you the choice — at(), std::span with hardening, debug-mode library assertions, sanitizers in testing — without charging code that doesn't need it.
